For the keyhole data the authors' code fixes the 18 test rows of its 80/20 split, and the supplement adds a test on SS316 after fitting on the other two alloys; srbf uses neither and splits the rows 80/20 anew in every run.
For the porosity data the authors report training and test scores without saying how they split the rows; srbf uses the random 80/20 split they state for the convection data.

srbf runs 2 of DRSR's 3 problems here (the DEBCat mass-luminosity data in linear and in log units): the synthetic mixture data set, half linear and half logistic at random, is not a function of x and is not run.
The authors do not say which stars they used; srbf takes both stars of every catalogued system that has a luminosity (324 stars), the selection that reproduces the scaling constants they print.
In the linear-units setting the authors rescale mass and luminosity to [0, 1] with constants they do not print; srbf uses both in solar units.

SLDBench poses 8 tasks, each asking for one law shared by all control groups of the task with constants refitted per group (the domain-mixture task predicts 5 losses at once); srbf runs each control group, and each of the 5 domain-mixture losses, as a separate problem.

srbf runs 14 of HeuristicLab's 376 problems here (the 5 real-world and 9 Miba friction datasets): 15 formula problems are in 'HeuristicLab regression instance providers' and 'HeuristicLab regression instance providers (fixed points)', 164 are run in other srbf sets (Keijzer, Korns, Nguyen, Vladislavleva, Feynman, ...), the 88 generated instances have no published formula, the 94 PennML datasets are run in SRBench, and AircraftMaximumLift has inputs without a range.

In the 9 Miba friction datasets the material, material category, grooving and oil inputs are letter codes; srbf turns each code into an input of its own that is 1 where the code applies and 0 elsewhere.

The authors pose one task per domain (chemistry, astrophysics, finance): one formula, with constants refitted per view, fitted to all its views at once; srbf runs each of the 20 views as a separate problem.

In the finance task the authors test the formulas found on the 10 company views by refitting them to the price-change histograms of 480 other companies and of the S&P 500; srbf rebuilt these 481 histograms with the authors' recipe (the authors publish only the resulting errors) and runs each as a problem of its own.

The authors published no data, only how they made them; srbf computed the six parton densities from the CT18NNLO grid on the authors' 20 x 20 training grid and their 20 test points at Q = 100 GeV, taking the details the text leaves open, such as where the test points lie in x, from the authors' own figures.

srbf runs 1 of the 3 problems of Desmond et al. (2023) (the observed SPARC data); the two MOND mock data sets, which place the authors' laws on the 2,696 observed baryonic accelerations rather than on a stated input range, are not run.

The authors give no values for the constants of the 80 chemistry and physics formulas. srbf fitted them to each problem's training data; with them every formula reproduces the authors' data to float32 precision. The values are srbf's reconstruction, not the authors'.

The authors write the time-series inputs as functions of time, A(t), and the chemistry constants as numbers joined to names, 0.19_z, which do not read as formulas, and print the exponent 1/3 as 0.333333333333333; srbf writes plain inputs, named constants and 1/3.

srbf follows the authors' data release: 240 problems, 44 of them in physics, named from 0, where the paper's Table 4 numbers from 1 (CRK0 is its CRK1) and the materials science names skip 15, 17, 26 and 27 (MatSci28 is its MatSci25). The paper's text counts 239 problems, 43 in physics.

In the materials science problems strain and temperature move together on one line (the temperature is 273 K plus 500 times the strain), so the data cannot separate a formula's dependence on each. srbf keeps them as published.

In 22 LSR-Synth problems (12 physics, 5 chemistry, 5 biology) the system has settled before the out-of-domain window: the targets there vary by less than 0.1% of their training spread, so the out-of-domain error mostly measures tiny absolute differences. srbf keeps them as published.
